player.name: Pell Wicklow
player.concept: a nosy gnome tinker-wizard with too many pockets and a habit of talking to animals

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Late afternoon settles over the crossroads. A weathered milestone stands beside the empty gibbet; blackthorn hedges crowd the drovers’ track, and crows pick at a dead ox in the ditch. Smoke tangles with the wind, though no hearth is in sight.

A mud-caked farmer jabs his pitchfork at the hedge, then shouts at the milestone. His red-rimmed eyes and unsteady laugh suggest he hasn’t slept. “You tell ’em, stone! Little green devils in the hedges—” He spots you and wheels around, leveling the pitchfork. “Stay back! I know what you are!”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I stop dead, raise both hands (one still holding a half-eaten pear) and waggle my fingers. "Easy, friend, easy! Pinkish, see? Not a speck of green on me, unless you count the moss stain on my left knee." I nod politely at the milestone. "What's the stone been telling you, then? I've always found milestones terrible conversationalists. All numbers, no gossip."

transcript.speaker: dice
transcript.text: Persuasion check: 15 + 1 = 16 vs DC 10: success

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Tam’s pitchfork dips. He grabs your sleeve with his free hand, then seems to realize he’s doing it and lets go.

“Right. Pinkish. Yes. You’ve got the look of a person who knows a stone can’t gossip.” His laugh comes out too loud. “Ox was theirs, though. Crude arrows in the poor beast, and little green devils slipping through the hedges after me since dawn. Told the tollhouse, I did. They said cider.”

He glances toward the blackthorn, then rubs the front of his smock as if checking something’s still there. “I only want to get home to Bet. Hollis Farm, down the track. You’ll believe me, won’t you?”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: "Hollis Farm!" I clap my hands, pear and all. "Hold on, not the Hollis with the weathervane shaped like a goose in a bonnet? I fixed that goose! Must be fifteen years back. Squeaked something awful in a westerly." I tap the side of my nose. "And Bet, is she your wife? Does she still make that plum tart with the burnt top?" I glance at his smock. "And you can stop patting your belly, friend. I'm not a pickpocket. Well. Not professionally."

transcript.speaker: dice
transcript.text: Insight check: 5 + 2 = 7 vs DC 12: failure

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Tam gives you a startled look, then a shaky nod. “Goose bonnet? Aye! Still squeaks, but Bet says it keeps the sparrows off. And the tart—well, burnt top’s the best bit, ain’t it?”

For a moment, the terror eases from his face. When you glance at his smock, he only gives a nervous little laugh. “Not patting my belly. Making sure my heart’s still in there, that’s all. Goblins’ll do that to a man.”

He tells you again about the arrows, the ox, the green shapes darting between the hedges. He seems frightened and sincere. “Walk with me to the farm? Please. Just till I’m home with Bet.”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: "Course I'll walk you home, Tam. Only, one moment." I trot over to the ditch and crouch a polite distance from the crows, holding out my pear core like a calling card. "Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen of the ditch. Fine ox. My condolences to the ox. I don't suppose any of you saw who put the arrows in him? I'd pay in pear." While I wait for an answer I squint at the arrows sticking out of the carcass.

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
The crows shuffle closer, bold as old landlords. One croaks, then another answers from the ox’s back. At your offer, the largest snatches the pear core and flaps up to the milestone.

The arrows are crude, short shafts of dark wood, fletched with ragged black feathers. The wounds around them are old enough that the blood has gone tacky.

Behind you, Tam says, “You’ll come with me, then? Bet’ll put the kettle on.” His hand drifts to the same spot beneath his smock. The crows suddenly lift as one, wings beating hard. From somewhere inside the blackthorn comes a dry, rattling sound.

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I straighten up slowly, motion for Tam to lower his pitchfork, and edge between him and the blackthorn. Then I cup my hands and call into the hedge in my rusty Goblin, which I picked up years ago swapping buttons with a tribe under the Mossfell bridge: "Hello in there! Peace! I'm not with the pitchfork. I'm a tinker. I have sweets, string, and a very good kettle-whistle, and I'd love to know your names."

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
For a beat, the hedge gives no answer. Then the rattle sounds again—closer, from the opposite side of the track.

A wiry goblin in a wolf-skin hood steps through the blackthorn, one ear missing, bone rattle raised. Four more shapes shift behind him, short bows aimed low but ready. “Skrag hears tinker-talk! Skrag says longlegs put down pointy stick.”

Tam’s pitchfork wavers behind you. The goblin’s yellow eyes flick to his smock. “Farmer has Grandmother Bone. Skrag wants her back. No quarrel with button-man—unless button-man makes quarrel.”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I give Skrag the Mossfell bow, one hand flat on my head and one on my belly, the way old Nettlegums taught me. "Skrag! An honour. Button-man makes no quarrel." Over my shoulder, gently: "Tam, set the pointy stick down, there's a love. Nobody's skewering anybody before supper." Back to Skrag, all eagerness: "Grandmother Bone. Is she a real grandmother? Yours? Tell me about her! And, oh, do you know Nettlegums, from under the Mossfell bridge? Three teeth, sings when she cheats at knucklebones?"

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Tam’s fingers clamp over the lump beneath his smock. “I ain’t got no grandmother in there,” he blurts, too quickly. “Just—just my own things.”

Skrag lowers the rattle a fraction, eyes narrowed at your greeting. “Nettlegums? Three-teeth cheat-witch? Skrag knows name. Nettlegums owes Skrag two buttons and a song.” His gaze returns to Tam. “Grandmother Bone belongs to warren. Farmer dug her from old dead place. Give her back.”

Tam looks from Skrag to you, frightened and ashamed. “I didn’t know she belonged to anyone. I only meant to sell her.” The goblins’ bows remain trained on the track, but Skrag waits. “Show Grandmother,” he says. “Then we talk.”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I pat Tam's elbow. "Nobody's cross with you, Tam. Well, Skrag is a bit, but he's being very civil about it." I lower my voice. "Let's show her, eh? Then we can all go have that kettle." Then, because I can't help myself: "Where was this old dead place you dug her from? A barrow? And what did you need the coin for, is the farm in a pinch?" I glance at the empty gibbet. "And who used to hang there, anyway? Nobody's swung from that in an age, by the rust."

transcript.speaker: dice
transcript.text: Insight check: 11 + 2 = 13 vs DC 12: success

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Tam’s fingers keep returning to the same hidden lump. This time you catch the flicker in his eyes: he knows the questions have found something.

With a sigh, he fishes a small bundle wrapped in rotten leather from his smock. Inside is a carved old woman, no bigger than your palm, her garnet eyes catching the late light. The air around it feels solemn, shrine-quiet.

“Found it in my field,” Tam insists, holding it close. “Finder’s keepers. I need the coin for a new ox.” Skrag’s rattling stops. “Grandmother Bone,” he breathes. “Home. Now.” Tam looks at you, torn. “You’d give away a good ox’s worth?”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I hold up a finger to each of them, like a schoolmistress. "Now hold on, both of you. Skrag, those are your folk's arrows in Tam's ox, aren't they? So the warren already owes Tam one ox. And Tam owes the warren one grandmother. Seems to me that's a trade waiting to happen." I turn to Skrag, curious. "What does she do for you, Grandmother Bone? Is she a guardian, a luck-charm, an actual ancestor? And what does the warren have that a farmer might want instead of coin? Mushrooms? Digging? Ox-sitting?"

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Skrag’s ears twitch at “arrows.” He glances toward the dead ox, then bares his teeth. “Ox was in the way. Arrows cost nothing.” A goblin behind him snickers; Skrag cuts it quiet with a look.

“Grandmother keeps the warren lucky,” he says, a little less theatrically now. “Keeps the dead-grandmothers listening. Without her, chief takes Skrag’s other ear.” His knife dips, though the bows stay ready.

Tam clutches the idol. “I need an ox. I can’t plough with mushrooms.” Skrag gives a sharp, impatient rattle. “No ox. We have mushrooms. We can dig, too—but not for free.” He looks between you and Tam. “You make a trade, button-man. What do you offer?”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I beam. "Here is my offer. Tam, I am a tinker-wizard. I will build you an ox. A clockwork ox!" I point at the empty gibbet. "Out of that. Iron's iron, and nobody's using it. Skrag's lot dig it up and haul it to Hollis Farm, I do the clever bits tonight, and by the weekend you've an ox that ploughs and never needs feeding. Skrag takes Grandmother home, and the warren throws in mushrooms for Bet." I start emptying my pockets onto the milestone: pliers, a coil of copper wire, three springs, a jar of grease, and a brass beetle that ticks.

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
The brass beetle ticks on the milestone. Skrag watches it, then the springs, then the gibbet. His goblins murmur among themselves; one points at the iron frame and whispers, “Big metal ox?”

Tam stares at you. “You can make an ox out of a gallows?” His grip loosens on the bundle, but he doesn’t let go. “And it’ll plough?”

Skrag lifts his rattle. “Skrag likes mushrooms. Skrag likes iron. But no iron ox tonight, no mushrooms today.” He points his knife at the idol. “Grandmother comes home first. Then Skrag talks trade.” Tam’s gaze turns to you, uncertain. “What do you say, Pell?”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: "I say it's fair, Tam. Grandmother first, then trade. Goblins remember who's polite." I hold out both palms to him. "Give her to me, and I'll hand her over proper. If Skrag welches, it's my ox-promise that's broken, not yours." If he gives her over, I carry the little carved woman to Skrag in both hands like a hot pie, and set her in his palms. "There. Home." Then I sniff the air and frown up at the grey smoke drifting over the hedges. "Skrag, is that your warren's cookfires I've been smelling all afternoon? Because I can't see a chimney anywhere."

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Skrag takes Grandmother Bone in both hands. For a moment, the theatrics drop from his face. He presses the little figure to his wolf-skin hood and murmurs something in goblin too soft to catch. Then he tucks her away carefully.

“Grandmother goes home,” he says. “Skrag remembers button-man’s promise.” His goblins lower their bows, though one eyes the gibbet hopefully. “Smoke? Burnt mill, north. Our cookfire. Mushrooms grow there—but iron ox is your clever-work, not ours.”

Tam watches Skrag turn toward the hedgerow, worry plain on his face. Skrag pauses and glances back. “You come to mill when ox is made. We trade mushrooms then.”

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Skrag cradles Grandmother Bone beneath his chin, then gives you a stiff, solemn nod. “Skrag remembers the iron ox,” he says, before he and his goblins melt into the blackthorn.

Tam watches them go, then lets out a breath that shakes into a laugh. “Well, that’s my ox gone twice over, then.” He looks at the ticking brass beetle on the milestone. “You really can build me one?”

transcript.speaker: system
transcript.text: Scene ends: Grandmother Bone goes home

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
The light has gone amber over the crossroads. Broken arrows litter the road; the dead ox lies in the ditch, and Tam’s pitchfork is abandoned where he dropped it. After a moment, Tam peers around the scarred milestone, then hurries over, hands still trembling.

“Saints and turnips, you’re all right? Nobody got a goblin spear in them?” He looks from face to face, relief and worry tumbling together. “You saved my hide. I—I’ll repay you somehow. Bet’ll feed you proper, if you’ll come to Hollis Farm. Or—” He glances north, where the tracks lead away. His smile falters. “They came from that way. The old burnt mill.”

history.summary: Previous scene, "The Mad Farmer at the Crossroads", ended: Grandmother Bone goes home. The goblins take the idol back and leave without a fight. Tam is safe but out of pocket.
